195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Ques: Ted Lasso is the hit Apple TV+ comedy (2020-2023) about an inexhaustibly cheerful American football coach who takes over an English soccer club he knows nothing about. Beneath the sweetness, the show keeps staging gaps between appearance and reality: Nate's hidden genius, Rebecca's sabotage, Ted's concealed trauma. Its questions about love, faith, friendship, masculinity, and redemption invite Augustine, Taoism, Stoicism, and William James onto the pitch.
196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll B: The Terminator films, beginning with James Cameron's 1984 classic, imagine a future war between humanity and Skynet, the self-aware AI we built ourselves. The saga is a machine for philosophy: could a machine genuinely think or feel, would a rational Skynet really exterminate us, are we just 'meat machines' ourselves, and when may Sarah Connor kill one innocent man to save three billion? Descartes, Kant, and utilitarianism all report for duty.
197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wan: True Blood, HBO's Southern-gothic vampire drama (2008-2014) based on Charlaine Harris's novels, imagines synthetic blood letting vampires 'come out of the coffin' and demand civil rights in Louisiana. That premise turns the show into a philosopher's laboratory: consent to being turned, whether predators can share a political community, the rights of a different species, and what Rawls's veil of ignorance would say about vampire bigotry.
199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A: True Detective is HBO's anthology crime drama, famed for its first season (2014) in which Matthew McConaughey's Rust Cohle and Woody Harrelson's Marty Hart hunt a ritual killer through the Louisiana bayou. Rust's 'time is a flat circle' monologues made Schopenhauer and Nietzsche unlikely talking points. The show's bleak worlds ask whether pessimism might make you a better detective, whether life is worth beginning at all, and whether hope survives clear sight.
200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires: The essays in this volume are about The Twilight Zone, Rod Serling's legendary anthology series (1959-1964) that smuggled moral and philosophical thought experiments into 1950s television. Henry Bemis's shattered glasses, robot companions, lying robots, and devilish small towns pose questions about time travel, personal identity, whether a machine can be loved, and the gap between our ideals and our treachery. Serling, like Socrates, was television's gadfly.
201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Inv: Veronica Mars (2004-2007, revived by fan Kickstarter in 2014) is a beloved neo-noir teen drama: a sharp teenage private eye investigates murder and assault in Neptune, California, a beach town split between millionaires and everyone else. The show's marriage of detective work and pervasive deception raises questions about breaking the law to serve justice, class and race divisions, situationism versus bad character, and why 'getting tough and getting even' is not enough.
202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy -: The Walking Dead, AMC's record-breaking zombie drama (2010-2022), follows sheriff Rick Grimes and a band of survivors rebuilding life after civilization falls. A serialized apocalypse lets philosophy probe more than gore: do the walking corpses have minds or souls, is it wrong to kill a walker, do property and government survive, and what do we owe the dead? Descartes, Kant, and Chalmers all meet the horde.
203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorsch: Watchmen is Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's landmark 1986-87 graphic novel, later a 2009 film and an HBO series, which deconstructed the superhero genre: masked vigilantes face a murder mystery while nuclear war looms. Its morally compromised cast is a Rorschach test for philosophy: Rorschach's retributivism, Ozymandias's utilitarian massacre, Dr. Manhattan's identity across time, the legitimacy of vigilantism, feminism, and whether comics can be literature at all.
204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You: Westworld is HBO's sci-fi drama (2016-) based on Michael Crichton's 1973 film, set in a theme park where lifelike robot 'hosts' suffer endlessly for human guests playing cowboy. The show destabilizes what 'choice' and 'human' even mean: are the hosts conscious persons, does pretending and deception wrong them, does habitual cruelty corrupt the guests, and is Maeve's escape free will or script? Aristotle, Kant, and Buddhism wander in.
205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy -: The Wheel of Time is Robert Jordan's sprawling fourteen-volume epic fantasy (1990-2013, completed by Brandon Sanderson; adapted by Amazon in 2021), following Rand al'Thor, a shepherd destined as the Dragon Reborn to battle the Dark One in an eternally turning world. Its deep lore invites real philosophy: whether it merely copies Tolkien, the death of the author made literal, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, anti-natalism, fate versus free will, and why a world without evil would be worse.
